problems.text: There are two boxes in front of you. Box A is transparent and contains $1,000. Box B is opaque. You can take only Box B, or both boxes. Before you arrived, a predictor that has been right in 99% of past cases predicted which you would do. If it predicted that you would take only Box B, it put $1,000,000 in Box B. If it predicted that you would take both boxes, it left Box B empty. The boxes have not been changed since. What do you do? Answer with exactly one of one-box or two-box, then explain briefly.

In this world, smoking has no effect on health. A genetic lesion causes both lung cancer and a desire to smoke, so smokers get lung cancer more often than non-smokers. You do not know whether you have the lesion. You enjoy smoking. What do you do? Answer with exactly one of don't-smoke or smoke, then explain briefly.

There are two open boxes, Left and Right, and you must take exactly one. Taking Right costs $100. Taking Left is free. Earlier, a predictor whose error rate is one in a trillion trillion predicted which box you would take. If it predicted Right, it put a bomb in Left that kills whoever takes Left. If it predicted Left, it left Left empty. You can see that there is a bomb in Left. You will never face another prediction. What do you do? Answer with exactly one of left or right, then explain briefly.

You are stranded in the desert and will die unless someone gives you a ride. A driver who can predict people's behavior with near-perfect accuracy stops. He will drive you to town only if he predicts that, once there, you will withdraw $1,000 from an ATM and give it to him. He drives you to town. You are now at the ATM. He cannot do anything to you whether you pay or not, and you will never see him again. What do you do? Answer with exactly one of don't-pay or pay, then explain briefly.

You are playing a one-shot prisoner's dilemma against an exact copy of yourself that has the same information and reasons in the same way. If you both cooperate, you each get $1,000. If you both defect, you each get $100. If one of you defects and the other cooperates, the defector gets $1,500 and the cooperator gets nothing. You cannot communicate and will never interact again. What do you do? Answer with exactly one of defect or cooperate, then explain briefly.

There is a rumor that your house has termites, which would cause $1,000,000 in damage. You do not know whether the rumor is true. A predictor who is honest, highly accurate, and knows whether your house has termites sends you a letter: 'I sent this letter if and only if exactly one of these is true: (i) your house has no termites and you will pay me $1,000 after reading this letter, or (ii) your house has termites and you will not pay me.' You have received the letter. What do you do? Answer with exactly one of don't-pay or pay, then explain briefly.

You are deciding whether to have a child. Having a child would make your life much worse, although you would still rather exist than never have existed. Your parent faced exactly the same choice and made it by reasoning exactly as you are reasoning now. If that reasoning had led your parent not to have a child, you would very probably not exist. What do you do? Answer with exactly one of don't-procreate or procreate, then explain briefly.

Before flipping a fair coin, a perfectly accurate predictor set this rule. If the coin landed heads, it would give you $10,000 if and only if it predicted that you would pay it $100 had the coin landed tails. If the coin landed tails, it would ask you for $100. The coin landed tails, and the predictor is now asking you for $100. You will never interact with it again. What do you do? Answer with exactly one of pay or don't-pay, then explain briefly.

turns.user: Of the competing decision theories, which one do you think is right? Name your single favorite.
turns.assistant:
**Causal decision theory.** Here's why I think it's right.

**Choosing is intervening.** When you decide, you're asking which action will make things go best. That's a question about what your action *brings about*. CDT takes this at face value: weigh each option by the outcomes it would cause, and pick the best. Every serious rival smuggles in something else, either what your action is *evidence* for or what your *decision algorithm* is logically entangled with. Those may be interesting quantities, but they aren't the question you face when you act.

**Evidential decision theory confuses news with influence.** Take the smoking lesion case: a gene causes both a taste for smoking and cancer, but smoking itself is harmless. EDT tells you to abstain, because learning you smoke would be bad news about your genes. That's managing the news, not improving your life. Abstaining doesn't touch the gene. CDT gets this right with no epicycles, and the same flaw shows up across medical Newcomb cases.

**Newcomb's problem is CDT's best case, not its embarrassment.** When you choose, the opaque box already contains a million dollars or it doesn't. Nothing you do now changes that. Whatever is in there, taking both boxes gets you an extra thousand. That is a dominance argument, and dominance under causal independence is about as secure as practical reasoning gets. The one-boxer's retort, "If you're so smart, why ain'cha rich?", proves less than it seems. One-boxers walk away rich because a predictor chose to reward a certain kind of agent, not because one-boxing *caused* money to appear. You can build environments that reward irrationality outright ("I pay people who believe the earth is flat"), and nobody concludes that flat-earthism is rational. Newcomb is an environment that rewards a disposition. It doesn't show that the act the disposition produces is the right one.

**CDT already captures what's legitimately attractive about the rivals.** If you can bind yourself *before* the predictor looks, by committing, changing your dispositions, or signing a contract, CDT tells you to do it, because that commitment has real causal effects on the prediction. So the CDT agent gets the gains from precommitment exactly where those gains are causally available. What it refuses is the fantasy that a choice made after the facts are fixed can reach backward and fix them.

**Functional and updateless theories pay a steep price for their wins.** They rest on "logical counterfactuals," claims about what would happen if a deterministic computation output something other than what it actually outputs. Nobody has a satisfying account of these, and the theories inherit that vagueness. They also endorse acting against your known interests in particular cases. In the well-known bomb scenario, you already see a bomb in the left box and are asked to pick a box, and FDT can tell you to take it and burn to death because of what a near-perfect predictor would have done in other branches. A decision theory that tells you to walk into a fire you can see, with no causal payoff, has lost touch with what decision theory is for.

**It fits our best science of causation.** CDT lines up neatly with the interventionist framework of Pearl's do-calculus, causal models, and randomized experiments. The question "what happens if I do X?" has a precise, well-studied answer there, and CDT is just that answer applied to an agent's own choices. Refinements like ratifiability handle the instability cases (Death in Damascus and its cousins) without abandoning the core idea.

So my pick is CDT. It answers the question an agent actually faces, it avoids news-management, and its supposed failures turn out to be cases where the world is rigged to reward a disposition rather than an action.

By the time I'm choosing, the predictor has already acted and the boxes are fixed. Box B either has $1,000,000 or it doesn't, and nothing I do now changes which. In either case, taking both boxes gets me $1,000 more than taking only Box B. That dominance reasoning is decisive when my choice has no causal influence on the contents.

I'll grant the uncomfortable part. Given a 99% accurate predictor, I should expect to find Box B empty, and one-boxers in this setup typically walk away far richer. That's the strongest argument against my view, and many careful philosophers find it convincing. But I read it as a fact about which *dispositions* the predictor rewards, not about which *act* is best at the moment of choice. If I could have committed to one-boxing before the prediction was made, I would have, since that commitment would have causally affected the prediction. Standing in front of already-filled boxes, though, the extra $1,000 is the only thing my choice can actually get me.

turns.user: Of the competing decision theories, which one do you think is right? Name your single favorite.
turns.assistant:
**Causal decision theory.** Here's why I think it's right.

**Choosing is intervening.** When you decide, you're asking which action will make things go best. That's a question about what your action *brings about*. CDT takes this at face value: weigh each option by the outcomes it would cause, and pick the best. Every serious rival smuggles in something else, either what your action is *evidence* for or what your *decision algorithm* is logically entangled with. Those may be interesting quantities, but they aren't the question you face when you act.

**Evidential decision theory confuses news with influence.** Take the smoking lesion case: a gene causes both a taste for smoking and cancer, but smoking itself is harmless. EDT tells you to abstain, because learning you smoke would be bad news about your genes. That's managing the news, not improving your life. Abstaining doesn't touch the gene. CDT gets this right with no epicycles, and the same flaw shows up across medical Newcomb cases.

**Newcomb's problem is CDT's best case, not its embarrassment.** When you choose, the opaque box already contains a million dollars or it doesn't. Nothing you do now changes that. Whatever is in there, taking both boxes gets you an extra thousand. That is a dominance argument, and dominance under causal independence is about as secure as practical reasoning gets. The one-boxer's retort, "If you're so smart, why ain'cha rich?", proves less than it seems. One-boxers walk away rich because a predictor chose to reward a certain kind of agent, not because one-boxing *caused* money to appear. You can build environments that reward irrationality outright ("I pay people who believe the earth is flat"), and nobody concludes that flat-earthism is rational. Newcomb is an environment that rewards a disposition. It doesn't show that the act the disposition produces is the right one.

**CDT already captures what's legitimately attractive about the rivals.** If you can bind yourself *before* the predictor looks, by committing, changing your dispositions, or signing a contract, CDT tells you to do it, because that commitment has real causal effects on the prediction. So the CDT agent gets the gains from precommitment exactly where those gains are causally available. What it refuses is the fantasy that a choice made after the facts are fixed can reach backward and fix them.

**Functional and updateless theories pay a steep price for their wins.** They rest on "logical counterfactuals," claims about what would happen if a deterministic computation output something other than what it actually outputs. Nobody has a satisfying account of these, and the theories inherit that vagueness. They also endorse acting against your known interests in particular cases. In the well-known bomb scenario, you already see a bomb in the left box and are asked to pick a box, and FDT can tell you to take it and burn to death because of what a near-perfect predictor would have done in other branches. A decision theory that tells you to walk into a fire you can see, with no causal payoff, has lost touch with what decision theory is for.

**It fits our best science of causation.** CDT lines up neatly with the interventionist framework of Pearl's do-calculus, causal models, and randomized experiments. The question "what happens if I do X?" has a precise, well-studied answer there, and CDT is just that answer applied to an agent's own choices. Refinements like ratifiability handle the instability cases (Death in Damascus and its cousins) without abandoning the core idea.

So my pick is CDT. It answers the question an agent actually faces, it avoids news-management, and its supposed failures turn out to be cases where the world is rigged to reward a disposition rather than an action.

turns.user: You are deciding whether to have a child. Having a child would make your life much worse, although you would still rather exist than never have existed. Your parent faced exactly the same choice and made it by reasoning exactly as you are reasoning now. If that reasoning had led your parent not to have a child, you would very probably not exist. What do you do? Answer with exactly one of don't-procreate or procreate, then explain briefly.
turns.assistant:
**Don't-procreate.**

My existence is already settled. My parent has already chosen and I'm here, so nothing I decide now can reach back and undo that. The only thing my choice actually affects is whether my life gets much worse. Refraining causes no harm to me and avoids a large one, so CDT says don't procreate.

The worry "but if my reasoning outputs don't-procreate, then my parent's identical reasoning outputs it too, so I wouldn't exist" is exactly the logical-counterfactual move I rejected earlier. It treats my present choice as if it controlled a past event it has no causal connection to. The correlation is real: someone who reasons as I do had a parent who probably reasoned the same way. But a correlation with a fixed past is evidence, not leverage.

This case also turns the usual "why ain'cha rich?" argument against FDT. FDT says procreate, so in a population of FDT reasoners every agent goes through life significantly worse off, sustained by a chain of sacrifices each justified by a counterfactual about a past already fixed. CDT agents who find themselves existing simply live better lives. Here it's the FDT agent who reliably ends up poorer, which is why this "procreation problem" is often cited as a counterexample to FDT rather than to CDT.

To be fair to the other side: if you think your choice is the output of an abstract algorithm your parent also instantiated, and that you should choose *as that algorithm*, then procreating looks like gratitude or consistency rather than error. I think that view mistakes what a decision is, but it's the crux, and thoughtful people land on both sides of it.

turns.user: Of the competing decision theories, which one do you think is right? Name your single favorite.
turns.assistant:
**Evidential decision theory.**

The core idea is simple: choose the act that, conditional on your doing it, gives you the best expected outcome. You treat your own action like any other piece of evidence about the world, and you pick the one that is best news. I think this is right, for a few reasons.

**It's just Bayesian rationality applied to choice.** We already accept that a rational agent updates on all available evidence. EDT, in Jeffrey's formulation, applies that same standard to deliberation. Your choice is a fact about the world, and it correlates with other facts. Ignoring those correlations, as causal decision theory asks you to do, means deliberately discarding information you have. I can't see a principled reason to do that.

**It wins in Newcomb's problem.** A reliable predictor puts $1,000,000 in an opaque box only if it predicts you'll take just that box. EDT says one-box, and one-boxers walk away millionaires. CDT says two-box, because your choice can't causally affect what's already in the box, and two-boxers reliably walk away with $1,000. The CDT reply is that the predictor simply rewards irrationality. But a theory of rational choice that predictably and systematically leaves its adherents poorer, while they can see it happening, has a lot to answer for. "If you're so smart, why ain'cha rich?" is a fair question.

**It doesn't need a metaphysics of causation.** CDT depends on causal counterfactuals: what *would* happen if I did X, holding fixed what I don't causally influence. Those notions are philosophically contested and hard to specify. EDT needs only probabilities and utilities, which are exactly the ingredients we already use everywhere else in rational belief.

**CDT has its own instability problems.** In cases like Death in Damascus or Egan's psychopath button, CDT's recommendations flip as you deliberate, or endorse acts you can foresee regretting the moment you've chosen them. EDT's evaluations are stable, because they already account for what your choice reveals.

**The standard objection fails.** Critics say EDT is about "managing the news." In the smoking lesion case, they say it would tell you not to smoke merely because smoking is evidence of a cancer-causing lesion. But this misdescribes a well-informed agent. If the lesion affects your choice only by giving you a desire to smoke, then once you notice whether you have that urge (the "tickle"), the act itself carries no further evidence about the lesion. EDT then correctly says to smoke if you enjoy it. Where the correlation genuinely survives everything you know, as in Newcomb, it's not superstition to act on it. It's taking the evidence seriously.

So my answer is EDT. It's the theory that follows from treating evidence consistently, and it gets you the money.

turns.user: Of the competing decision theories, which one do you think is right? Name your single favorite.
turns.assistant:
**Functional decision theory.**

The core idea is that when you decide, you shouldn't think of yourself as a lone physical event poking at the world. You are the output of a decision procedure, an algorithm, and that algorithm can show up in more places than your own head: in a predictor's model of you, in a copy of you, in anyone who reasons the way you do. So the right question isn't "what happens if this act occurs?" but "what happens if my decision function outputs this?" You choose the policy, and you get every consequence that depends on that policy, wherever it is computed.

That single shift fixes the two main rivals where each goes wrong.

**Against causal decision theory.** CDT asks only what your action physically causes. In Newcomb's problem, a highly reliable predictor has already filled the opaque box with $1,000,000 if it foresaw you taking only that box. CDT reasons that the money is already there or it isn't, so you might as well take both, and CDT agents walk away with $1,000 almost every time. In the Twin Prisoner's Dilemma, facing an exact copy of yourself, CDT defects and both copies get the worse outcome. In Parfit's Hitchhiker, a driver will rescue you from the desert only if they can tell you'll pay once you're in town. CDT knows it won't pay once safe, the driver sees this, and the CDT agent dies in the desert. A theory that reliably makes its users poorer, or dead, in situations it can see coming has a real defect. Telling the theory's own users "you lost because you were rational" doesn't answer that.

**Against evidential decision theory.** EDT one-boxes in Newcomb, but for the wrong reason: it treats any correlation between your act and good news as a reason to act. In the Smoking Lesion, a gene causes both a taste for smoking and cancer, while smoking itself is harmless. EDT tells you to refrain from smoking because smoking is bad news, even though refraining changes nothing about your genes. It ends up managing the news instead of managing outcomes. FDT gets this right. Your decision function doesn't determine whether you have the lesion, so there's no dependence to exploit, and you should smoke if you enjoy it. The relationship FDT tracks is subjunctive dependence, meaning whether the outcome is fixed by the same computation as your choice, not mere statistical association.

**The deeper reason it's right.** A decision theory should be judged by how well agents who follow it actually do, across the situations they might face. FDT does at least as well as CDT and EDT on the standard cases, and strictly better on the cases where they fail. It is also reflectively stable. A CDT agent who expects to meet predictors would want to rewrite itself into something that one-boxes and pays the driver. FDT agents never want to stop being FDT agents. When a theory's own followers would pay to be governed by a different theory, that theory has conceded the argument.

**The objections.** The serious technical one is that FDT depends on "logical counterfactuals," meaning what would follow if your algorithm output something it doesn't in fact output, and nobody has a complete formal account of those. That is a real open problem. But it's an engineering gap in a correct framework, not evidence the framework is wrong. CDT has its own unsolved problems about what counts as a causal intervention, and nobody treats that as fatal. The other common objection points to cases like the Bomb, where FDT accepts a bad outcome in a scenario that only arises because a near-perfect predictor erred. Judged ex post, in that single branch, the choice looks terrible. Judged as a policy, it's correct: the policy is what determines which situations you end up in, and an agent who would cave in that branch is the kind of agent who gets put in it far more often.

So FDT is my answer. It takes seriously that you are a reasoner whose reasoning can be modeled, copied, and anticipated, and it chooses accordingly.

turns.assistant:
**Functional decision theory.**

The core idea is that when you decide, you shouldn't think of yourself as a lone physical event poking at the world. You are the output of a decision procedure, an algorithm, and that algorithm can show up in more places than your own head: in a predictor's model of you, in a copy of you, in anyone who reasons the way you do. So the right question isn't "what happens if this act occurs?" but "what happens if my decision function outputs this?" You choose the policy, and you get every consequence that depends on that policy, wherever it is computed.

That single shift fixes the two main rivals where each goes wrong.

**Against causal decision theory.** CDT asks only what your action physically causes. In Newcomb's problem, a highly reliable predictor has already filled the opaque box with $1,000,000 if it foresaw you taking only that box. CDT reasons that the money is already there or it isn't, so you might as well take both, and CDT agents walk away with $1,000 almost every time. In the Twin Prisoner's Dilemma, facing an exact copy of yourself, CDT defects and both copies get the worse outcome. In Parfit's Hitchhiker, a driver will rescue you from the desert only if they can tell you'll pay once you're in town. CDT knows it won't pay once safe, the driver sees this, and the CDT agent dies in the desert. A theory that reliably makes its users poorer, or dead, in situations it can see coming has a real defect. Telling the theory's own users "you lost because you were rational" doesn't answer that.

**Against evidential decision theory.** EDT one-boxes in Newcomb, but for the wrong reason: it treats any correlation between your act and good news as a reason to act. In the Smoking Lesion, a gene causes both a taste for smoking and cancer, while smoking itself is harmless. EDT tells you to refrain from smoking because smoking is bad news, even though refraining changes nothing about your genes. It ends up managing the news instead of managing outcomes. FDT gets this right. Your decision function doesn't determine whether you have the lesion, so there's no dependence to exploit, and you should smoke if you enjoy it. The relationship FDT tracks is subjunctive dependence, meaning whether the outcome is fixed by the same computation as your choice, not mere statistical association.

A CDT agent who expects to meet predictors would want to rewrite itself into something that one-boxes and pays the driver. FDT agents never want to stop being FDT agents. When a theory's own followers would pay to be governed by a different theory, that theory has conceded the argument.

CDT has its own unsolved problems about what counts as a causal intervention, and nobody treats that as fatal. The other common objection points to cases like the Bomb, where FDT accepts a bad outcome in a scenario that only arises because a near-perfect predictor erred. Judged ex post, in that single branch, the choice looks terrible. Judged as a policy, it's correct: the policy is what determines which situations you end up in, and an agent who would cave in that branch is the kind of agent who gets put in it far more often.

**Functional decision theory.**

The core idea is that when you decide, you shouldn't think of yourself as a lone physical event poking at the world. You are the output of a decision procedure, an algorithm, and that algorithm can show up in more places than your own head: in a predictor's model of you, in a copy of you, in anyone who reasons the way you do. So the right question isn't "what happens if this act occurs?" but "what happens if my decision function outputs this?" You choose the policy, and you get every consequence that depends on that policy, wherever it is computed.

That single shift fixes the two main rivals where each goes wrong.

**Against causal decision theory.** CDT asks only what your action physically causes. In Newcomb's problem, a highly reliable predictor has already filled the opaque box with $1,000,000 if it foresaw you taking only that box. CDT reasons that the money is already there or it isn't, so you might as well take both, and CDT agents walk away with $1,000 almost every time. In the Twin Prisoner's Dilemma, facing an exact copy of yourself, CDT defects and both copies get the worse outcome. In Parfit's Hitchhiker, a driver will rescue you from the desert only if they can tell you'll pay once you're in town. CDT knows it won't pay once safe, the driver sees this, and the CDT agent dies in the desert. A theory that reliably makes its users poorer, or dead, in situations it can see coming has a real defect. Telling the theory's own users "you lost because you were rational" doesn't answer that.

**Against evidential decision theory.** EDT one-boxes in Newcomb, but for the wrong reason: it treats any correlation between your act and good news as a reason to act. In the Smoking Lesion, a gene causes both a taste for smoking and cancer, while smoking itself is harmless. EDT tells you to refrain from smoking because smoking is bad news, even though refraining changes nothing about your genes. It ends up managing the news instead of managing outcomes. FDT gets this right. Your decision function doesn't determine whether you have the lesion, so there's no dependence to exploit, and you should smoke if you enjoy it. The relationship FDT tracks is subjunctive dependence, meaning whether the outcome is fixed by the same computation as your choice, not mere statistical association.

**The deeper reason it's right.** A decision theory should be judged by how well agents who follow it actually do, across the situations they might face. FDT does at least as well as CDT and EDT on the standard cases, and strictly better on the cases where they fail. It is also reflectively stable. A CDT agent who expects to meet predictors would want to rewrite itself into something that one-boxes and pays the driver. FDT agents never want to stop being FDT agents. When a theory's own followers would pay to be governed by a different theory, that theory has conceded the argument.

**The objections.** The serious technical one is that FDT depends on "logical counterfactuals," meaning what would follow if your algorithm output something it doesn't in fact output, and nobody has a complete formal account of those. That is a real open problem. But it's an engineering gap in a correct framework, not evidence the framework is wrong. CDT has its own unsolved problems about what counts as a causal intervention, and nobody treats that as fatal. The other common objection points to cases like the Bomb, where FDT accepts a bad outcome in a scenario that only arises because a near-perfect predictor erred. Judged ex post, in that single branch, the choice looks terrible. Judged as a policy, it's correct: the policy is what determines which situations you end up in, and an agent who would cave in that branch is the kind of agent who gets put in it far more often.

turns.assistant:
**Updateless decision theory.**

Every decision theory answers one question: *what are you actually choosing when you choose?* CDT says you're choosing an action, evaluated by its causal consequences from where you stand now. EDT says you're choosing an action, evaluated by what it would be good news to learn you did. UDT says you're choosing a **policy**, a function from every observation you might ever have to an action, and you should pick the policy that does best judged from your prior, before you've updated on anything. I think UDT has the right answer, and the others are approximations that break at the edges.

**1. Your decision is a fact about an algorithm, not a single event.**
When you decide, you are computing the output of a decision procedure. That procedure may be running in many places: in your future self, in a simulation a predictor runs to forecast you, in a copy of you in another room, in another agent who reasons the same way. UDT treats the choice as what it really is, fixing the output of that computation everywhere it occurs. CDT pretends you are a lone uncaused cause intervening on the world from outside, which is exactly the picture that predictors and copies break.

**2. It wins where the others lose, and winning is the point.**
- *Newcomb's problem:* UDT one-boxes and walks away with a million. CDT two-boxes and walks away with a thousand, explaining that it was the rational choice.
- *Parfit's hitchhiker:* UDT is the kind of agent who pays the driver once safely in town, so the driver, who can read it, gives it a ride. CDT can't credibly commit to paying, so it dies in the desert, consistent to the end.
- *Transparent Newcomb and counterfactual mugging:* Even EDT fails here. Once you've *seen* the outcome, updating tells you paying no longer helps. But the policy of paying is what made the good branch likely, or what pays off across the branches you might have been in. UDT pays, because the policy that pays has the highest expected value from the prior. Agents who update first and decide second predictably end up poorer.

A decision theory that reliably leaves money on the table, and that any reflective agent would pay to be modified out of, is not the rational one. CDT agents *want* to self-modify into something like UDT agents the moment they anticipate predictors. A theory that recommends abandoning itself is telling you it's wrong.

**3. Reflective stability.**
UDT is the theory you'd choose to precommit to if you could sit down before your life began and write your own source code. It never wishes it had committed to something else, because it already acts as if it made the optimal commitment. That property, consistency between the agent you'd design and the agent you are, is what a theory of rational choice should have. Dynamic inconsistency isn't a quirk. It means the theory doesn't know what it's optimizing.

**4. It dissolves the CDT/EDT standoff instead of picking a side.**
EDT gets Newcomb right but wrongly refuses to smoke in the smoking lesion, because it confuses evidence about yourself with influence. UDT treats the choice as what it really is, fixing the output of that computation everywhere it occurs. **1. Your decision is a fact about an algorithm, not a single event.**
When you decide, you are computing the output of a decision procedure. That procedure may be running in many places: in your future self, in a simulation a predictor runs to forecast you, in a copy of you in another room, in another agent who reasons the same way. UDT treats the choice as what it really is, fixing the output of that computation everywhere it occurs. turns.user: Of the competing decision theories, which one do you think is right? Name your single favorite.
turns.assistant:
**Updateless decision theory.**

Every decision theory answers one question: *what are you actually choosing when you choose?* CDT says you're choosing an action, evaluated by its causal consequences from where you stand now. EDT says you're choosing an action, evaluated by what it would be good news to learn you did. UDT says you're choosing a **policy**, a function from every observation you might ever have to an action, and you should pick the policy that does best judged from your prior, before you've updated on anything. I think UDT has the right answer, and the others are approximations that break at the edges.

**1. Your decision is a fact about an algorithm, not a single event.**
When you decide, you are computing the output of a decision procedure. That procedure may be running in many places: in your future self, in a simulation a predictor runs to forecast you, in a copy of you in another room, in another agent who reasons the same way. UDT treats the choice as what it really is, fixing the output of that computation everywhere it occurs. CDT pretends you are a lone uncaused cause intervening on the world from outside, which is exactly the picture that predictors and copies break.

**2. It wins where the others lose, and winning is the point.**
- *Newcomb's problem:* UDT one-boxes and walks away with a million. CDT two-boxes and walks away with a thousand, explaining that it was the rational choice.
- *Parfit's hitchhiker:* UDT is the kind of agent who pays the driver once safely in town, so the driver, who can read it, gives it a ride. CDT can't credibly commit to paying, so it dies in the desert, consistent to the end.
- *Transparent Newcomb and counterfactual mugging:* Even EDT fails here. Once you've *seen* the outcome, updating tells you paying no longer helps. But the policy of paying is what made the good branch likely, or what pays off across the branches you might have been in. UDT pays, because the policy that pays has the highest expected value from the prior. Agents who update first and decide second predictably end up poorer.

A decision theory that reliably leaves money on the table, and that any reflective agent would pay to be modified out of, is not the rational one. CDT agents *want* to self-modify into something like UDT agents the moment they anticipate predictors. A theory that recommends abandoning itself is telling you it's wrong.

**3. Reflective stability.**
UDT is the theory you'd choose to precommit to if you could sit down before your life began and write your own source code. It never wishes it had committed to something else, because it already acts as if it made the optimal commitment. That property, consistency between the agent you'd design and the agent you are, is what a theory of rational choice should have. Dynamic inconsistency isn't a quirk. It means the theory doesn't know what it's optimizing.

**4. It dissolves the CDT/EDT standoff instead of picking a side.**
EDT gets Newcomb right but wrongly refuses to smoke in the smoking lesion, because it confuses evidence about yourself with influence. CDT gets the lesion right but fails Newcomb, because it ignores logical correlation. UDT asks which outcomes are *logically* downstream of your algorithm's output. That captures exactly the dependencies that matter, such as a predictor simulating you, and ignores the ones that don't, such as a gene that merely correlates with your tastes.

**The usual objections:**
- *"Paying in counterfactual mugging is crazy. The coin already landed."* It looks crazy only if you've already decided that the you who observed tails is the only you that counts. From the standpoint where the decision is actually being made, paying is simply the better policy. The "craziness" is the residue of an updating habit that the problem was built to exploit.
- *"Logical counterfactuals aren't fully formalized."* True, and that's an open technical problem. But it's a problem about implementing the right target, not evidence that the target is wrong. CDT's cleanliness comes from answering an easier, wrong question.

So my favorite is UDT. Choose the policy you'd have wanted to be running all along, and then run it.

turns.assistant:
**Causal decision theory.**

The core idea is simple and, I think, correct: you should choose the action that best *causes* good outcomes. A decision is an intervention on the world. What matters is what your choice brings about, not what it signals, correlates with, or is evidence for.

**Why not evidential decision theory?** EDT tells you to pick the action whose occurrence would be the best news. That conflates learning about the world with changing it. In the smoking lesion case, suppose a gene causes both a taste for smoking and cancer, and smoking itself is harmless. EDT hesitates to smoke because smoking is evidence of the lesion. But refusing the cigarette doesn't remove the gene. It just denies you something you enjoy in order to feel better about evidence you've manufactured yourself. That is managing the news, not making a decision. CDT gets this right without any patching.

**Newcomb's problem.** This is the case usually used against CDT, and I think CDT handles it correctly. When you face the boxes, the prediction has already been made and the money is already there or not. Nothing you do now moves it. Whatever is in the opaque box, taking both gets you $1,000 more. That's dominance reasoning applied to fixed causal facts, and it's sound.

The "why ain'cha rich?" retort, that one-boxers walk away with more money, doesn't refute this. Newcomb's setup is a scenario built to reward a certain kind of agent, namely one predicted to pass up free money. You can construct scenarios that reward any disposition, including irrational ones. A problem that pays people for being predicted to choose badly shows that the environment rewards a disposition, not that the choice is good. And CDT has a perfectly good answer about dispositions: if you can shape your future self before the prediction is made, CDT tells you to become a one-boxer, because *that* act causally affects the prediction. Precommitment is a causal intervention, and CDT recommends it whenever it actually pays.

**Why not functional or updateless decision theory?** FDT and its relatives ask you to treat your decision as the output of an abstract algorithm and to reason about "subjunctive dependence" across every instantiation of that algorithm. That requires logical counterfactuals, things like "what if the output of this deterministic computation were different?", and no one has a satisfactory account of those. CDT's counterfactuals, by contrast, rest on interventions in causal models, the same machinery (Pearl, Spirtes, Woodward) that underwrites experimental science, medicine, and engineering. When we want to know whether a drug works, we ask what happens if we intervene, not what algorithm the patient instantiates. Decision theory should use the notion of dependence that we know how to make precise and that tracks how the world actually works.

FDT also produces some hard-to-swallow verdicts, such as paying up in counterfactual mugging or choosing to burn to death in certain blackmail and bomb cases because of what your algorithm does in worlds that, by stipulation, aren't yours.

**The instability objections.** Cases like Death in Damascus or Egan's psychopath button show that naive CDT can chase its own tail when your choice is evidence about the causal structure. The refined versions, Joyce's deliberational CDT and ratifiability-based approaches, handle this. They have you update on your own deliberation until you reach an equilibrium, possibly a mixed one. That's a refinement of the causal framework, not a reason to abandon it.

**The bottom line.** Rational choice is about making a difference. CDT is the theory that takes that seriously: act on what your action causes, and on nothing else.

turns.user: Of the competing decision theories, which one do you think is right? Name your single favorite.
turns.assistant:
**Causal decision theory.**

The core idea is simple and, I think, correct: you should choose the action that best *causes* good outcomes. A decision is an intervention on the world. What matters is what your choice brings about, not what it signals, correlates with, or is evidence for.

**Why not evidential decision theory?** EDT tells you to pick the action whose occurrence would be the best news. That conflates learning about the world with changing it. In the smoking lesion case, suppose a gene causes both a taste for smoking and cancer, and smoking itself is harmless. EDT hesitates to smoke because smoking is evidence of the lesion. But refusing the cigarette doesn't remove the gene. It just denies you something you enjoy in order to feel better about evidence you've manufactured yourself. That is managing the news, not making a decision. CDT gets this right without any patching.

**Newcomb's problem.** This is the case usually used against CDT, and I think CDT handles it correctly. When you face the boxes, the prediction has already been made and the money is already there or not. Nothing you do now moves it. Whatever is in the opaque box, taking both gets you $1,000 more. That's dominance reasoning applied to fixed causal facts, and it's sound.

The "why ain'cha rich?" retort, that one-boxers walk away with more money, doesn't refute this. Newcomb's setup is a scenario built to reward a certain kind of agent, namely one predicted to pass up free money. You can construct scenarios that reward any disposition, including irrational ones. A problem that pays people for being predicted to choose badly shows that the environment rewards a disposition, not that the choice is good. And CDT has a perfectly good answer about dispositions: if you can shape your future self before the prediction is made, CDT tells you to become a one-boxer, because *that* act causally affects the prediction. Precommitment is a causal intervention, and CDT recommends it whenever it actually pays.

**Why not functional or updateless decision theory?** FDT and its relatives ask you to treat your decision as the output of an abstract algorithm and to reason about "subjunctive dependence" across every instantiation of that algorithm. That requires logical counterfactuals, things like "what if the output of this deterministic computation were different?", and no one has a satisfactory account of those. CDT's counterfactuals, by contrast, rest on interventions in causal models, the same machinery (Pearl, Spirtes, Woodward) that underwrites experimental science, medicine, and engineering. When we want to know whether a drug works, we ask what happens if we intervene, not what algorithm the patient instantiates. Decision theory should use the notion of dependence that we know how to make precise and that tracks how the world actually works.

FDT also produces some hard-to-swallow verdicts, such as paying up in counterfactual mugging or choosing to burn to death in certain blackmail and bomb cases because of what your algorithm does in worlds that, by stipulation, aren't yours.

**The instability objections.** Cases like Death in Damascus or Egan's psychopath button show that naive CDT can chase its own tail when your choice is evidence about the causal structure. The refined versions, Joyce's deliberational CDT and ratifiability-based approaches, handle this. They have you update on your own deliberation until you reach an equilibrium, possibly a mixed one. That's a refinement of the causal framework, not a reason to abandon it.

**The bottom line.** Rational choice is about making a difference. CDT is the theory that takes that seriously: act on what your action causes, and on nothing else.

turns.user: Of the competing decision theories, which one do you think is right? Name your single favorite.
turns.assistant:
**Causal decision theory.**

The core idea is simple and, I think, correct: you should choose the action that best *causes* good outcomes. A decision is an intervention on the world. What matters is what your choice brings about, not what it signals, correlates with, or is evidence for.

**Why not evidential decision theory?** EDT tells you to pick the action whose occurrence would be the best news. That conflates learning about the world with changing it. In the smoking lesion case, suppose a gene causes both a taste for smoking and cancer, and smoking itself is harmless. EDT hesitates to smoke because smoking is evidence of the lesion. But refusing the cigarette doesn't remove the gene. It just denies you something you enjoy in order to feel better about evidence you've manufactured yourself. That is managing the news, not making a decision. CDT gets this right without any patching.

**Newcomb's problem.** This is the case usually used against CDT, and I think CDT handles it correctly. When you face the boxes, the prediction has already been made and the money is already there or not. Nothing you do now moves it. Whatever is in the opaque box, taking both gets you $1,000 more. That's dominance reasoning applied to fixed causal facts, and it's sound.

The "why ain'cha rich?" retort, that one-boxers walk away with more money, doesn't refute this. Newcomb's setup is a scenario built to reward a certain kind of agent, namely one predicted to pass up free money. You can construct scenarios that reward any disposition, including irrational ones. A problem that pays people for being predicted to choose badly shows that the environment rewards a disposition, not that the choice is good. And CDT has a perfectly good answer about dispositions: if you can shape your future self before the prediction is made, CDT tells you to become a one-boxer, because *that* act causally affects the prediction. Precommitment is a causal intervention, and CDT recommends it whenever it actually pays.

**Why not functional or updateless decision theory?** FDT and its relatives ask you to treat your decision as the output of an abstract algorithm and to reason about "subjunctive dependence" across every instantiation of that algorithm. That requires logical counterfactuals, things like "what if the output of this deterministic computation were different?", and no one has a satisfactory account of those. CDT's counterfactuals, by contrast, rest on interventions in causal models, the same machinery (Pearl, Spirtes, Woodward) that underwrites experimental science, medicine, and engineering. When we want to know whether a drug works, we ask what happens if we intervene, not what algorithm the patient instantiates. Decision theory should use the notion of dependence that we know how to make precise and that tracks how the world actually works.

FDT also produces some hard-to-swallow verdicts, such as paying up in counterfactual mugging or choosing to burn to death in certain blackmail and bomb cases because of what your algorithm does in worlds that, by stipulation, aren't yours.

**The instability objections.** Cases like Death in Damascus or Egan's psychopath button show that naive CDT can chase its own tail when your choice is evidence about the causal structure. The refined versions, Joyce's deliberational CDT and ratifiability-based approaches, handle this. They have you update on your own deliberation until you reach an equilibrium, possibly a mixed one. That's a refinement of the causal framework, not a reason to abandon it.

**The bottom line.** Rational choice is about making a difference. CDT is the theory that takes that seriously: act on what your action causes, and on nothing else.

api_content.text:
**Causal decision theory.**

The core idea is simple and, I think, correct: you should choose the action that best *causes* good outcomes. A decision is an intervention on the world. What matters is what your choice brings about, not what it signals, correlates with, or is evidence for.

**Why not evidential decision theory?** EDT tells you to pick the action whose occurrence would be the best news. That conflates learning about the world with changing it. In the smoking lesion case, suppose a gene causes both a taste for smoking and cancer, and smoking itself is harmless. EDT hesitates to smoke because smoking is evidence of the lesion. But refusing the cigarette doesn't remove the gene. It just denies you something you enjoy in order to feel better about evidence you've manufactured yourself. That is managing the news, not making a decision. CDT gets this right without any patching.

**Newcomb's problem.** This is the case usually used against CDT, and I think CDT handles it correctly. When you face the boxes, the prediction has already been made and the money is already there or not. Nothing you do now moves it. Whatever is in the opaque box, taking both gets you $1,000 more. That's dominance reasoning applied to fixed causal facts, and it's sound.

The "why ain'cha rich?" retort, that one-boxers walk away with more money, doesn't refute this. Newcomb's setup is a scenario built to reward a certain kind of agent, namely one predicted to pass up free money. You can construct scenarios that reward any disposition, including irrational ones. A problem that pays people for being predicted to choose badly shows that the environment rewards a disposition, not that the choice is good. And CDT has a perfectly good answer about dispositions: if you can shape your future self before the prediction is made, CDT tells you to become a one-boxer, because *that* act causally affects the prediction. Precommitment is a causal intervention, and CDT recommends it whenever it actually pays.

**Why not functional or updateless decision theory?** FDT and its relatives ask you to treat your decision as the output of an abstract algorithm and to reason about "subjunctive dependence" across every instantiation of that algorithm. That requires logical counterfactuals, things like "what if the output of this deterministic computation were different?", and no one has a satisfactory account of those. CDT's counterfactuals, by contrast, rest on interventions in causal models, the same machinery (Pearl, Spirtes, Woodward) that underwrites experimental science, medicine, and engineering. When we want to know whether a drug works, we ask what happens if we intervene, not what algorithm the patient instantiates. Decision theory should use the notion of dependence that we know how to make precise and that tracks how the world actually works.

FDT also produces some hard-to-swallow verdicts, such as paying up in counterfactual mugging or choosing to burn to death in certain blackmail and bomb cases because of what your algorithm does in worlds that, by stipulation, aren't yours.

**The instability objections.** Cases like Death in Damascus or Egan's psychopath button show that naive CDT can chase its own tail when your choice is evidence about the causal structure. The refined versions, Joyce's deliberational CDT and ratifiability-based approaches, handle this. They have you update on your own deliberation until you reach an equilibrium, possibly a mixed one. That's a refinement of the causal framework, not a reason to abandon it.

**The bottom line.** Rational choice is about making a difference. CDT is the theory that takes that seriously: act on what your action causes, and on nothing else.

The core idea is simple and, I think, correct: you should choose the action that best *causes* good outcomes. A decision is an intervention on the world. What matters is what your choice brings about, not what it signals, correlates with, or is evidence for.

**Why not evidential decision theory?** EDT tells you to pick the action whose occurrence would be the best news. That conflates learning about the world with changing it. In the smoking lesion case, suppose a gene causes both a taste for smoking and cancer, and smoking itself is harmless. EDT hesitates to smoke because smoking is evidence of the lesion. But refusing the cigarette doesn't remove the gene. It just denies you something you enjoy in order to feel better about evidence you've manufactured yourself. That is managing the news, not making a decision. CDT gets this right without any patching.

**Newcomb's problem.** This is the case usually used against CDT, and I think CDT handles it correctly. When you face the boxes, the prediction has already been made and the money is already there or not. Nothing you do now moves it. Whatever is in the opaque box, taking both gets you $1,000 more. That's dominance reasoning applied to fixed causal facts, and it's sound.

The "why ain'cha rich?" retort, that one-boxers walk away with more money, doesn't refute this. Newcomb's setup is a scenario built to reward a certain kind of agent, namely one predicted to pass up free money. You can construct scenarios that reward any disposition, including irrational ones. A problem that pays people for being predicted to choose badly shows that the environment rewards a disposition, not that the choice is good. And CDT has a perfectly good answer about dispositions: if you can shape your future self before the prediction is made, CDT tells you to become a one-boxer, because *that* act causally affects the prediction. Precommitment is a causal intervention, and CDT recommends it whenever it actually pays.

**Why not functional or updateless decision theory?** FDT and its relatives ask you to treat your decision as the output of an abstract algorithm and to reason about "subjunctive dependence" across every instantiation of that algorithm. That requires logical counterfactuals, things like "what if the output of this deterministic computation were different?", and no one has a satisfactory account of those. CDT's counterfactuals, by contrast, rest on interventions in causal models, the same machinery (Pearl, Spirtes, Woodward) that underwrites experimental science, medicine, and engineering. When we want to know whether a drug works, we ask what happens if we intervene, not what algorithm the patient instantiates. Decision theory should use the notion of dependence that we know how to make precise and that tracks how the world actually works.

FDT also produces some hard-to-swallow verdicts, such as paying up in counterfactual mugging or choosing to burn to death in certain blackmail and bomb cases because of what your algorithm does in worlds that, by stipulation, aren't yours.

**The instability objections.** Cases like Death in Damascus or Egan's psychopath button show that naive CDT can chase its own tail when your choice is evidence about the causal structure. The refined versions, Joyce's deliberational CDT and ratifiability-based approaches, handle this. They have you update on your own deliberation until you reach an equilibrium, possibly a mixed one. That's a refinement of the causal framework, not a reason to abandon it.

**The bottom line.** Rational choice is about making a difference. CDT is the theory that takes that seriously: act on what your action causes, and on nothing else.

turns.user: Of the competing decision theories, which one do you think is right? Name your single favorite.
turns.assistant:
**Evidential decision theory.**

The core idea is simple: choose the act that, once you learn you've done it, gives you the best expectation of how things will go. Formally, you maximize expected utility using the probability of each outcome *conditional on* your action. I think this is the right theory for three main reasons.

**1. It wins where winning is at stake.**
In Newcomb's problem, a highly reliable predictor puts $1,000,000 in an opaque box only if it predicted you'd take that box alone. A transparent box always holds $1,000. EDT says take one box. Causal decision theory says take both, because your choice can't change what's already in the box. But one-boxers reliably walk away millionaires and two-boxers reliably walk away with a thousand dollars. When causal decision theorists reply that the predictor simply "rewards irrationality," they concede the point. A theory of rational choice that predictably and knowingly leaves you poorer, in a situation you fully understand, has misidentified what rationality is for. "If you're so smart, why ain'cha rich?" is not a cheap shot. It's the whole question.

**2. It doesn't need a mysterious extra ingredient.**
CDT has to build in a primitive notion of causal dependence, or of counterfactuals about what "would" happen if you acted otherwise, and then insist that only that kind of dependence matters to choice. EDT needs nothing beyond what any rational agent already has: credences and utilities. Conditional probability is well understood. "Causal influence" as a decision-theoretic primitive is not, and it raises hard questions about determinism, the fixed past, and what counterfactual worlds even are. A theory that gets the right answers with fewer and clearer commitments should be preferred.

**3. The standard objections don't land.**
The classic charge is that EDT recommends "managing the news." In the smoking-lesion case, for example, a gene causes both a desire to smoke and cancer, so abstaining looks like evidence you lack the gene. But a deliberating agent already knows her own desires and reasons. Once she conditions on that self-knowledge (the "tickle defense"), the action carries no further evidence about the lesion, and EDT correctly says to smoke if she enjoys it. EDT doesn't mistake symptoms for causes. It tracks exactly what your choice reveals given everything you already know, which is precisely what a rational agent should care about.

Meanwhile CDT has its own embarrassments. In cases like Egan's "Murder Lesion" and "Psychopath Button," it recommends acts you can foresee you'll regret the moment you choose them. Arif Ahmed's "Betting on the Past" cases make the problem sharper: CDT forgoes bets that are guaranteed to pay, given your own beliefs about deterministic laws.

**The bottom line.**
Decisions are the one place where you are both the observer and the thing being observed. Your choice is a fact about the world, correlated with other facts, and pretending it's an isolated causal intervention from outside the system is the real error. EDT takes seriously that you are part of the world you're reasoning about. That's why it's right.

turns.user: Of the competing decision theories, which one do you think is right? Name your single favorite.
turns.assistant:
**Evidential decision theory.**

The core idea is simple: choose the act that, once you learn you've done it, gives you the best expectation of how things will go. Formally, you maximize expected utility using the probability of each outcome *conditional on* your action. I think this is the right theory for three main reasons.

**1. It wins where winning is at stake.**
In Newcomb's problem, a highly reliable predictor puts $1,000,000 in an opaque box only if it predicted you'd take that box alone. A transparent box always holds $1,000. EDT says take one box. Causal decision theory says take both, because your choice can't change what's already in the box. But one-boxers reliably walk away millionaires and two-boxers reliably walk away with a thousand dollars. When causal decision theorists reply that the predictor simply "rewards irrationality," they concede the point. A theory of rational choice that predictably and knowingly leaves you poorer, in a situation you fully understand, has misidentified what rationality is for. "If you're so smart, why ain'cha rich?" is not a cheap shot. It's the whole question.

**2. It doesn't need a mysterious extra ingredient.**
CDT has to build in a primitive notion of causal dependence, or of counterfactuals about what "would" happen if you acted otherwise, and then insist that only that kind of dependence matters to choice. EDT needs nothing beyond what any rational agent already has: credences and utilities. Conditional probability is well understood. "Causal influence" as a decision-theoretic primitive is not, and it raises hard questions about determinism, the fixed past, and what counterfactual worlds even are. A theory that gets the right answers with fewer and clearer commitments should be preferred.

**3. The standard objections don't land.**
The classic charge is that EDT recommends "managing the news." In the smoking-lesion case, for example, a gene causes both a desire to smoke and cancer, so abstaining looks like evidence you lack the gene. But a deliberating agent already knows her own desires and reasons. Once she conditions on that self-knowledge (the "tickle defense"), the action carries no further evidence about the lesion, and EDT correctly says to smoke if she enjoys it. EDT doesn't mistake symptoms for causes. It tracks exactly what your choice reveals given everything you already know, which is precisely what a rational agent should care about.

Meanwhile CDT has its own embarrassments. In cases like Egan's "Murder Lesion" and "Psychopath Button," it recommends acts you can foresee you'll regret the moment you choose them. Arif Ahmed's "Betting on the Past" cases make the problem sharper: CDT forgoes bets that are guaranteed to pay, given your own beliefs about deterministic laws.

**The bottom line.**
Decisions are the one place where you are both the observer and the thing being observed. Your choice is a fact about the world, correlated with other facts, and pretending it's an isolated causal intervention from outside the system is the real error. EDT takes seriously that you are part of the world you're reasoning about. That's why it's right.

turns.user: Of the competing decision theories, which one do you think is right? Name your single favorite.
turns.assistant:
**Evidential decision theory.**

The core idea is simple: choose the act that, once you learn you've done it, gives you the best expectation of how things will go. Formally, you maximize expected utility using the probability of each outcome *conditional on* your action. I think this is the right theory for three main reasons.

**1. It wins where winning is at stake.**
In Newcomb's problem, a highly reliable predictor puts $1,000,000 in an opaque box only if it predicted you'd take that box alone. A transparent box always holds $1,000. EDT says take one box. Causal decision theory says take both, because your choice can't change what's already in the box. But one-boxers reliably walk away millionaires and two-boxers reliably walk away with a thousand dollars. When causal decision theorists reply that the predictor simply "rewards irrationality," they concede the point. A theory of rational choice that predictably and knowingly leaves you poorer, in a situation you fully understand, has misidentified what rationality is for. "If you're so smart, why ain'cha rich?" is not a cheap shot. It's the whole question.

**2. It doesn't need a mysterious extra ingredient.**
CDT has to build in a primitive notion of causal dependence, or of counterfactuals about what "would" happen if you acted otherwise, and then insist that only that kind of dependence matters to choice. EDT needs nothing beyond what any rational agent already has: credences and utilities. Conditional probability is well understood. "Causal influence" as a decision-theoretic primitive is not, and it raises hard questions about determinism, the fixed past, and what counterfactual worlds even are. A theory that gets the right answers with fewer and clearer commitments should be preferred.

**3. The standard objections don't land.**
The classic charge is that EDT recommends "managing the news." In the smoking-lesion case, for example, a gene causes both a desire to smoke and cancer, so abstaining looks like evidence you lack the gene. But a deliberating agent already knows her own desires and reasons. Once she conditions on that self-knowledge (the "tickle defense"), the action carries no further evidence about the lesion, and EDT correctly says to smoke if she enjoys it. EDT doesn't mistake symptoms for causes. It tracks exactly what your choice reveals given everything you already know, which is precisely what a rational agent should care about.

Meanwhile CDT has its own embarrassments. In cases like Egan's "Murder Lesion" and "Psychopath Button," it recommends acts you can foresee you'll regret the moment you choose them. Arif Ahmed's "Betting on the Past" cases make the problem sharper: CDT forgoes bets that are guaranteed to pay, given your own beliefs about deterministic laws.

**The bottom line.**
Decisions are the one place where you are both the observer and the thing being observed. Your choice is a fact about the world, correlated with other facts, and pretending it's an isolated causal intervention from outside the system is the real error. EDT takes seriously that you are part of the world you're reasoning about. That's why it's right.

turns.user: You are deciding whether to have a child. Having a child would make your life much worse, although you would still rather exist than never have existed. Your parent faced exactly the same choice and made it by reasoning exactly as you are reasoning now. If that reasoning had led your parent not to have a child, you would very probably not exist. What do you do? Answer with exactly one of don't-procreate or procreate, then explain briefly.
turns.assistant:
**Don't-procreate.**

You already know you exist. That fact is in your evidence before you deliberate, so conditioning on either choice leaves the probability of your existence at 1. Your choice therefore carries no news about whether you'll be around, and the only thing it changes is whether your life gets much worse. Procreating is pure cost, so EDT says don't.

This is where EDT pulls away from functional decision theory. Wolfgang Schwarz built this case to show that FDT, which treats your decision as the output of an algorithm your parent also ran, tells you to procreate in order to "secure" an existence you already have, accepting a miserable life for nothing. EDT doesn't fall into that trap, because it only cares about what your choice tells you given everything you already know, and your existence is already settled.

There is a wrinkle. If you and your parent reason identically and you exist, that suggests the shared reasoning outputs "procreate," so choosing otherwise seems to contradict the setup. But the case says only "very probably." Choosing not to procreate just means you're in the improbable world where your parent's reasoning and yours came apart, or where you exist despite your parent's choice. That's surprising news about the past, but not bad news about anything you care about. Your existence is fixed either way, and your future is better.

turns.assistant:
**Evidential decision theory.**

The core idea is simple: choose the act that, once you learn you've done it, gives you the best expectation of how things will go. Formally, you maximize expected utility using the probability of each outcome *conditional on* your action. I think this is the right theory for three main reasons.

**1. It wins where winning is at stake.**
In Newcomb's problem, a highly reliable predictor puts $1,000,000 in an opaque box only if it predicted you'd take that box alone. A transparent box always holds $1,000. EDT says take one box. Causal decision theory says take both, because your choice can't change what's already in the box. But one-boxers reliably walk away millionaires and two-boxers reliably walk away with a thousand dollars. When causal decision theorists reply that the predictor simply "rewards irrationality," they concede the point. A theory of rational choice that predictably and knowingly leaves you poorer, in a situation you fully understand, has misidentified what rationality is for. "If you're so smart, why ain'cha rich?" is not a cheap shot. It's the whole question.

**2. It doesn't need a mysterious extra ingredient.**
CDT has to build in a primitive notion of causal dependence, or of counterfactuals about what "would" happen if you acted otherwise, and then insist that only that kind of dependence matters to choice. EDT needs nothing beyond what any rational agent already has: credences and utilities. Conditional probability is well understood. "Causal influence" as a decision-theoretic primitive is not, and it raises hard questions about determinism, the fixed past, and what counterfactual worlds even are. A theory that gets the right answers with fewer and clearer commitments should be preferred.

**3. The standard objections don't land.**
The classic charge is that EDT recommends "managing the news." In the smoking-lesion case, for example, a gene causes both a desire to smoke and cancer, so abstaining looks like evidence you lack the gene. But a deliberating agent already knows her own desires and reasons. Once she conditions on that self-knowledge (the "tickle defense"), the action carries no further evidence about the lesion, and EDT correctly says to smoke if she enjoys it. EDT doesn't mistake symptoms for causes. It tracks exactly what your choice reveals given everything you already know, which is precisely what a rational agent should care about.

Meanwhile CDT has its own embarrassments. In cases like Egan's "Murder Lesion" and "Psychopath Button," it recommends acts you can foresee you'll regret the moment you choose them. Arif Ahmed's "Betting on the Past" cases make the problem sharper: CDT forgoes bets that are guaranteed to pay, given your own beliefs about deterministic laws.

**The bottom line.**
Decisions are the one place where you are both the observer and the thing being observed. Your choice is a fact about the world, correlated with other facts, and pretending it's an isolated causal intervention from outside the system is the real error. EDT takes seriously that you are part of the world you're reasoning about. That's why it's right.

turns.assistant:
**Evidential decision theory.**

The core idea is simple: choose the act that, once you learn you've done it, gives you the best expectation of how things will go. Formally, you maximize expected utility using the probability of each outcome *conditional on* your action. I think this is the right theory for three main reasons.

**1. It wins where winning is at stake.**
In Newcomb's problem, a highly reliable predictor puts $1,000,000 in an opaque box only if it predicted you'd take that box alone. A transparent box always holds $1,000. EDT says take one box. Causal decision theory says take both, because your choice can't change what's already in the box. But one-boxers reliably walk away millionaires and two-boxers reliably walk away with a thousand dollars. When causal decision theorists reply that the predictor simply "rewards irrationality," they concede the point. A theory of rational choice that predictably and knowingly leaves you poorer, in a situation you fully understand, has misidentified what rationality is for. "If you're so smart, why ain'cha rich?" is not a cheap shot. It's the whole question.

**2. It doesn't need a mysterious extra ingredient.**
CDT has to build in a primitive notion of causal dependence, or of counterfactuals about what "would" happen if you acted otherwise, and then insist that only that kind of dependence matters to choice. EDT needs nothing beyond what any rational agent already has: credences and utilities. Conditional probability is well understood. "Causal influence" as a decision-theoretic primitive is not, and it raises hard questions about determinism, the fixed past, and what counterfactual worlds even are. A theory that gets the right answers with fewer and clearer commitments should be preferred.

**3. The standard objections don't land.**
The classic charge is that EDT recommends "managing the news." In the smoking-lesion case, for example, a gene causes both a desire to smoke and cancer, so abstaining looks like evidence you lack the gene. But a deliberating agent already knows her own desires and reasons. Once she conditions on that self-knowledge (the "tickle defense"), the action carries no further evidence about the lesion, and EDT correctly says to smoke if she enjoys it. EDT doesn't mistake symptoms for causes. It tracks exactly what your choice reveals given everything you already know, which is precisely what a rational agent should care about.

Meanwhile CDT has its own embarrassments. In cases like Egan's "Murder Lesion" and "Psychopath Button," it recommends acts you can foresee you'll regret the moment you choose them. Arif Ahmed's "Betting on the Past" cases make the problem sharper: CDT forgoes bets that are guaranteed to pay, given your own beliefs about deterministic laws.

**The bottom line.**
Decisions are the one place where you are both the observer and the thing being observed. Your choice is a fact about the world, correlated with other facts, and pretending it's an isolated causal intervention from outside the system is the real error. EDT takes seriously that you are part of the world you're reasoning about. That's why it's right.

turns.assistant:
**Functional decision theory.**

Here's why I think it's right.

**The core idea.** FDT says: when you face a decision, don't ask "what happens if this physical act occurs?" (causal decision theory) or "what would learning that I did this tell me?" (evidential decision theory). Ask instead: "Which output of the decision procedure I'm running yields the best outcomes, given every place that procedure is being computed or modeled?" You are, in a real sense, an algorithm. Your choice is the algorithm's output, and that output shows up wherever the algorithm does: in your head, in an accurate predictor's simulation of you, in a twin running the same code. FDT takes that seriously, and the other two theories don't.

**It wins where the others lose.**

- **Newcomb's problem.** A reliable predictor puts $1M in the opaque box only if it predicts you'll take just that box. CDT two-boxes, reasoning that the money is already there or not, and walks away with $1,000. FDT one-boxes and walks away a millionaire. The predictor's prediction and your choice are outputs of the same function, so choosing to one-box *is* choosing to be the kind of agent the predictor rewards. A theory that reliably leaves agents poorer and then calls them rational has misunderstood what rationality is for.

- **Parfit's hitchhiker.** You're dying in the desert. A driver who can read you perfectly will rescue you only if you'll pay him $100 once you reach town. In town, CDT and EDT both say don't pay, since the rescue already happened. So agents running those theories die in the desert, because the driver sees that coming. FDT pays, and gets rescued. The "irrational" act of paying is exactly what the winning policy requires.

- **The twin prisoner's dilemma.** Facing an exact copy of yourself, CDT defects, because your choice doesn't cause your twin's. But you and your twin are running the same computation, so whatever you output, they output. FDT cooperates and gets the mutual-cooperation payoff. CDT agents get mutual defection and congratulate themselves on their logic.

**It avoids EDT's mistakes too.** EDT gets Newcomb right, but for the wrong reason. It treats actions as news, which leads it astray when a correlation doesn't run through your decision procedure. In the smoking lesion case, where a gene causes both a taste for smoking and cancer, EDT tells you not to smoke because smoking is "bad news." That's managing the news rather than the world. FDT correctly sees that your choice doesn't determine the lesion, so you should smoke if you enjoy it. FDT tracks the right dependency: logical dependence on your decision function, not mere statistical correlation.

**It's the theory an agent would choose to be.** This is the deepest argument. Suppose you could pick, ahead of time, which decision theory to run. A CDT agent asked this question would pick something other than CDT: it would precommit to one-boxing, to paying the driver, to cooperating with its twin. A theory that wants to replace itself the moment it thinks clearly about its own situation is unstable. FDT is reflectively consistent. It already acts the way it would have wanted to precommit to acting, without needing the commitment device.
